text: You time the serial program, then the parallel one. Speedup is \(S = {{c1::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/T_{\mathrm{parallel} } }}\).
extra: Run times change with input size, but speedup changes much less, so the course talks about performance in terms of speedup.

text: You split the work evenly over \(p\) cores and pay no overhead at all. That best case is linear speedup, \(S = {{c1::p}}\), and it {{c2::almost never}} happens in practice.
extra: Linear means 2 cores run twice as fast, 4 cores four times as fast, and so on.

text: Efficiency tells you how much speedup each core contributes: \(E = {{c1::S/p}} = {{c2::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/(p \cdot T_{\mathrm{parallel} }) }}\).
extra: Lecture 14 also calls it the fraction of parallel run time each core spends on the actual problem. Linear speedup gives \(E = 1\).

text: Thread management, critical sections, mutex calls, network I/O, and file I/O all slow a parallel program down. These overheads {{c1::grow}} as you add threads or processes.
extra: That is why real speedup curves bend below the straight line \(S = p\).

text: As you add processors, speedup {{c1::increases}} but efficiency {{c2::decreases}}. Each extra processor buys you less than the one before it.
extra: Lecture 14's table has \(S = 6.5\) at 8 cores and \(S = 10.8\) at 16 cores, while \(E\) drops from 0.81 to 0.675.

text: With overhead included, parallel run time is \(T_{\mathrm{parallel} } = {{c1::T_{\mathrm{serial} }/p + T_{\mathrm{overhead} } }}\).
extra: The first term is the ideal split. The second is the time spent managing the parallel work.

text: Make the problem bigger and the overhead usually grows {{c1::more slowly}} than \(T_{\mathrm{serial} }\). So with a bigger problem, speedup and efficiency both {{c2::increase}}.
extra: The cores do more real work, so the overhead becomes a smaller share of the total.

text: A 20 s program is 90% parallelizable and the parallel part scales perfectly. On \(p\) cores it takes {{c1::\(18/p + 2\)}} seconds, because only the 18 s part shrinks.
extra: The 2 s serial part never gets faster, no matter how many cores you add.

text: Amdahl's law with serial fraction \(a\) says \(S = {{c1::1/((1-a)/p + a) }}\).
extra: The parallel part \(1-a\) is divided by \(p\). The serial part \(a\) stays the same.

text: Under Amdahl, adding cores forever only pushes speedup toward {{c1::\(1/a\)}}. A program that is 90% parallelizable never beats a speedup of {{c2::10}}.
extra: At 95% parallelizable the cap is 20. At 99% it is 100.

text: Amdahl's law tells you {{c1::superlinear}} speedup, meaning better than \(S = p\), will not come from parallelization.
extra: If the whole program is parallelizable, Amdahl gives exactly \(S = p\) and no more.

text: Measure how much of your run is serial, and Amdahl gives you the {{c1::maximum}} number of cores worth paying for. Past that point, more hardware buys almost nothing.
extra: The lecture frames this as a cost and benefit decision about how much hardware or cloud compute to buy.

text: A job takes 100 s on 1 core, 40 s on 4 cores, and 25 s on 8 cores. Speedup goes from 2.5 to {{c1::4}}, and efficiency drops from {{c2::0.625}} to {{c3::0.5}}.
extra: \(S = 100/40\) and \(100/25\). \(E = 2.5/4\) and \(4/8\). This is study guide practice question 5, answer A.
